🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.40% (intraday, 7-year +20bp). At trading day 7 (last close) it was -0.85% against a five-campaign average of -0.13% at the same point — only 2022-23 was worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +21bp since the hike vs a +2bp campaign average at the same point.
  • Stocks: US stocks fell under 1%; Europe was flat; Japan slipped 0.73%.
  • FX: The dollar firmed a little and the euro stayed weak; yen was unchanged.
  • Technicals: US indexes are unusually far above their long-run average; that's stretched, not broken.
  • Sectors: Defensive sectors held up; consumer, media and bank stocks led losses.
  • Credit/Spreads: Extra pay for corporate bond risk is near historic lows but edged up.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate: government debt and Iran/oil are the main risks.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is sticky and price rises are widespread; not re-accelerating yet.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip stocks are priced near 2000 levels; the broad market is far less stretched.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron reports Wednesday; options price a big move. Oura and Accelevation IPOs are coming.
  • Iran: Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz offer; talks may resume; oil flows through the strait increased.
  • Warsh: Fed raised rates in September; October pause likely, December hike possible.
  • Week Ahead: PCE inflation and GDP Wednesday, factory survey Thursday, jobs report Friday.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term: rising yields and pricey chip stocks could spark a pullback.
  • Trades: Trim Nasdaq exposure, buy protection on junk bonds, favor dollar and energy.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 sell, 23 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +1.18 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 100th pctile, +0bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Bond yields are driving this market; respect them until inflation cools.

The biggest story is rising long-term yields. The US 10-year closed at 5.2361% (+7.57bp) and the 2-year at 4.9305% (+7.89bp), with Bunds (+4.2bp) and Gilts (+5.6bp) also higher. US stocks, which had been at stretched levels, sold off: the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to 7683.69, the Nasdaq Composite 0.92% to 26820.38, the Dow 0.67% and the Russell 2000 0.69%. VIX rose 1.2 points to 16.07. Europe was flat (STOXX 600 +0.005%, Euro Stoxx 50 -0.02%) and the Nikkei fell 0.73%. The prior session's mood was complacent (VIX 14.87). Today was a modest de-risking rather than a panic. Credit spreads widened slightly (US HY +0.12, EM +0.08) from near-record tights. Brent gained 1.52% to 105.91 as Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz proposal. Silver fell 5.68%, copper 1.96% and natural gas 3.69%, so the metals move looks like liquidation rather than growth fear. Sentiment is cautious. The Fed's September hike to 3.75–4.0% and Wednesday's PCE report keep rates in charge.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Mini-cycle ranks are percentiles of SMA7/SMA14 and SMA50/SMA200 against each ETF's own history (no look-ahead). Dip odds are the share of past days in the same condition that saw a 5% drop within 3 months; 'ep' = distinct past episodes. The conditions are historical analogs, not validated signals. Full study: Mini-cycles-Findings.pdf (credit_mini_cycles skill).

Globally the pattern matches: Info Tech YTD +34.32, Energy +32.36, Cons Discr -9.25, and Materials -8.56 over 1 month. Growth (tech) is still the leader, but breadth is narrowing: cyclicals and rate-sensitive value are both being sold, leaving tech and energy.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. This rule failed all three pre-registered gates as a tradable overlay (placebo p=0.465); do not size positions off it. See the monitor_spread skill (MONITOR_SPREAD.md).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.18 vol points (93th percentile of the 29 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.8 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 43bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.24 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Sticky, but not re-accelerating. Headline core PCE YoY is 3.34%, well above target, and breadth is poor. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed dashboard points to one bubble and many tinderboxes. Semiconductor valuations are the true 2000 analogue, and Micron's print on Wednesday is the test: guidance for revenue of $50bn ±$1bn and EPS of $31 ±$1 is priced for perfection. Market-wide froth is well below the 78% Nasdaq drawdown setup of 2000–02 (peak 5048.62 on 2000-03-10). The current Oct-2022-anchored path is still on the early leg of the dotcom analogue. The more dangerous readings are in credit and liquidity: IG and Baa spreads are tighter than in 2000, and financial conditions are looser. The trigger in 2000 was Fed tightening into a narrow leadership group, and today the Fed is hiking with the 10Y at 5.24%. The retail survey is bearish, which argues against an imminent blow-off top. Analyst-estimate fields (top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth 45, LT EPS growth 70) were not verified by a web search this run; treat them as approximate.

⚔️Iran War

Day 213 of the conflict (GlobalSecurity, Sep 28). President Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks, though he expects talks to resume this week (CBS News). Iranian President Pezeshkian told CBS that Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors as part of a long-term ceasefire deal, despite an 'atmosphere of distrust'. Trump has not ruled out more strikes before the November midterms. The National reports the US and Iran will hold 'separate talks' with mediators. At sea, CENTCOM called Iran's claim to have seized a second US underwater drone in Hormuz 'clearly desperate' (Al Jazeera). Trump told Axios that more than 20 million barrels transited the strait over the weekend, the most since the war began. No new Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia was reported between the Sep 27–28 cutoffs, ending a three-day run of fire on Riyadh and Khamis Mushait. Market read: Brent +1.52% to 105.91 reflects the rejected proposal. Improving flows through Hormuz cap the upside unless strikes resume.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

October FOMC: a hold with a hawkish bias is the likelier outcome (inference). The FOMC just hiked 25bp unanimously to 3.75–4.0% in September, and the credible case for passing is time to observe that hike's effects. A hot August core PCE (Wednesday) plus a firm payrolls print would raise the odds of a back-to-back hike.

~1 YEAR

Inference from Warsh's record: one to two more 25bp hikes (J.P. Morgan forecasts December) followed by a prolonged hold rather than a long hiking cycle. The emphasis would be on regime change, including balance-sheet reduction, which adds term-premium pressure on the long end. Cuts are unlikely until underlying inflation 'meaningfully improves'.

At Jackson Hole, Warsh said underlying inflation has not 'meaningfully improved' and the Fed has 'work to do'. Analysts said the speech raised hike odds and could put the Fed 'at odds' with Treasury. In the Sep 16 press conference, he attributed higher 10-year yields to economic strength, competition for capital and geopolitics, which signals tolerance for higher long rates. CNBC (Sep 25) reports his 'regime change' agenda, including the balance sheet, is pushing ahead but meeting resistance inside the Fed. Core PCE above 3% every month of 2026 (our data: 3.34%) keeps him hawkish, while contained wages (AHE 3.1%) argue against an open-ended cycle. The forward-path calls are our inference, not Warsh's statements.

Sources: Kevin Warsh Says There's Still 'Work to Do' to Fight Inflation (Chase) · Jackson Hole analyst roundup: Warsh's speech sends hike chances higher (CNBC, 2026-08-31) · Warsh's regime change at the Fed pushes ahead – and meets resistance (CNBC, 2026-09-25) · What's The Fed's Next Move?
